passages.text: Some Lithuanian ethnobotanical taxa: a linguistic view on Thorn Apple and related plants
Background
The perception and use of plants correspond with common plant names. <sentence_start/>The study of plant names may give insight into historical and recent use of plants.
Methods

Plant names in dictionaries and folklore have been evaluated. <sentence_start/>A etymological analysis of the names is provided. <sentence_start/>Onomasiological and semasiological aspects have been considered. <sentence_start/>Therefore, species named with names related to each other have been selected.
Results

Plant names containing the stem <italic toggle="yes">dag</italic>- or <italic toggle="yes">deg</italic>- may belong to either of two categories: incenses or thorny plants. <sentence_start/>Plants named in <italic toggle="yes">durn</italic>- have been in use as psychopharmaca. <sentence_start/>The name <italic toggle="yes">rymo </italic>points not to Rome but to the use of plants as anodyne or psychopharmaca.
Background

The study of plant names is a quite old branche in ethnobotany. <sentence_start/>It is connected with comparative historical linguistics and Indo-European studies [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B1" count="1">1</citation>] or philological studies of singular languages, e.g. the dictionary of German plant names [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B2" count="1">2</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Names correspond with the perception and categorisation of plants. <sentence_start/>This is true for the binary scientific names [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B3" count="1">3</citation>] as well as for common plant names.

Linguistic studies have shown that plant names of common origin may refer to different plant species. <sentence_start/>E.g. Latin <italic toggle="yes">fāgus </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">Fagus </italic>sp.' vs. Old Greek <italic toggle="yes">phēgós </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">Quercus </italic>sp.'. <sentence_start/>Various explanations have been given, the most frequent is probably the missing of a certain plant in the area where speakers of a language came to settle. <sentence_start/>Another view points to an open question: we do not know what the reconstructed Indo-European *<italic toggle="yes">bhago</italic>- really meant. <sentence_start/>It could name <italic toggle="yes">Fagus </italic>sp. as well as any tree with leaves or hard timber [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B4" count="1">4</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B5" count="1">5</citation>].
Methods

Lithuanian plant names have been selected from written sources and common use. <sentence_start/>A philological analysis of the names has been provided, their botanical meaning has been discussed. <sentence_start/>Both, semasiological and onomasiological aspects have been considered. <sentence_start/>Therefore, species with identical or similar names have been selected for the present study. <sentence_start/>The etymological analysis is related with plant names from neighbouring Slavic and Germanic languages. <sentence_start/>It is supposed that names correspond with the use of these plants in traditional medicine, rites and handicrafts. <sentence_start/>Ethnographic data about plants have been an important source for the study. <sentence_start/>Due to requirements of linguistic papers we italicise not only botanical taxa but also linguistic forms. <sentence_start/>We hope that this will not result in confusion. <sentence_start/>Diacritics have been omitted.
Results and discussion
Durna

<italic toggle="yes">Durnaropė </italic>ist the most popular Lithuanian name for <italic toggle="yes">Datura stramonium</italic>. <sentence_start/>It is also used for recently introduced ornamental plants of the genus <italic toggle="yes">Brugmannsia</italic>. <sentence_start/>Other names for <italic toggle="yes">D. stramonium </italic>are <italic toggle="yes">durnadagilis</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">durnadagis</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">durnarėjus</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">durnažolė</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">durniukas </italic>etc. [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B6" count="1">6</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B7" count="1">7</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Linguists compare these terms usually with Russian <italic toggle="yes">durman </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">D. stramonium</italic>' and <italic toggle="yes">durnyj </italic>'stupid' and claim that the Lithuanian plantnames and Lithuanian <italic toggle="yes">durnas </italic>'stupid' have been borrowed from Slavic languages [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B8" count="1">8</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The origin of <italic toggle="yes">D. stramonium </italic>remains unclear until now. <sentence_start/>The species is indigenous either to Central America or to Asia or cosmopolitan. <sentence_start/>No sure evidence (palynolonogy, macro fossils) for neither views has been provided so far. <sentence_start/>It seems rather impossible to falsify one of these opinions. <sentence_start/>Therefore, linguistic discussion has no firm basis when it regards only this species. <sentence_start/>Additionally, there are other plants named in a similar way: <italic toggle="yes">durnažolė</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">durnius </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">Hyoscyamus niger </italic>L.', <italic toggle="yes">durnažolė </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">Atropa bella-donna </italic>L.', <italic toggle="yes">durnarepka </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">Scopolia carniolica </italic>Jacq.' and <italic toggle="yes">durnažolė </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">Lolium temulentum </italic>L.' [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B6" count="1">6</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B9" count="1">9</citation>]. <sentence_start/>All species are psychoactive. <sentence_start/>No doubt, the names refer explicitly to this effort. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">Hyoscyamus niger </italic>and <italic toggle="yes">Lolium temulentum </italic>are indigenous plants or at least archeophyts.

The use of psychoactive plants is a human universality and-generally speaking-not a matter of loaning. <sentence_start/>If plant names in <italic toggle="yes">durn</italic>- were loans then there should be synonymous names with Lithuanian <italic toggle="yes">paikas</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">kvailas</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">žioplas</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">trenktas </italic>etc. 'stupid, crazy'. <sentence_start/>In fact, only a single <italic toggle="yes">žioplys </italic>'idiot' appears for <italic toggle="yes">D. stramonium</italic>. <sentence_start/>Not only therefore, the conclusion is that <italic toggle="yes">durnas </italic>'stupid' is not a loan but Baltic heritage, however, cognate with the Slavic words for narcotic plants, e.g. Russian <italic toggle="yes">durman</italic>, Belorussian <italic toggle="yes">durzilje </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">D. stramonium</italic>', Russian <italic toggle="yes">durnišnik </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">Xanthium </italic>L.', Ukrainian <italic toggle="yes">dur </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">Hyoscyamus niger</italic>' [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B7" count="1">7</citation>].

A considerable number of Lithuanian phrases concern henbane, thorn apple etc. and their well known effort: "The drunkard gambols like having consumed henbane", "he talks nonsens as if he would have eaten thorn apple", "he turns around as if he would have consumed thorn apple" etc. [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B10" count="1">10</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The effort is temporary and primarily not a matter of character or intellect. <sentence_start/>Therefore, it is suggested that the original meaning of <italic toggle="yes">durnas </italic>etc. was not 'stupid' but 'drunken, high'. <sentence_start/>The use of psychoactive plants belongs to the responsibility of religion in quite a lot of cultures [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B11" count="1">11</citation>]. <sentence_start/>One can suppose that pre-Christian local religions used them as well. <sentence_start/>A hint is the name <italic toggle="yes">dievažolynis </italic>'God's herb' for <italic toggle="yes">D. stramonium </italic>[<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B10" count="1">10</citation>], where <italic toggle="yes">dievas </italic>'God' is probably the Pagan god of heaven, predecessor of the Christian God, for the Catholic rite do not favour the use of narcotic plants.
Rymo

Several Lithuanian plant names contain the word <italic toggle="yes">Rymo</italic>: <italic toggle="yes">Rymo ridikas</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">Rymo ropikės </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">Atropa bella-donna </italic>L.', <italic toggle="yes">Rymo ropė </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">Datura stramonium </italic>L.' and '<italic toggle="yes">Scopolia carniolica </italic>Jacq.', <italic toggle="yes">Rymo ramunė </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">Matricaria recutita </italic>L.' [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B6" count="1">6</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B10" count="1">10</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The spelling shows that <italic toggle="yes">Rymo </italic>has been understood as proper name: <italic toggle="yes">Rymo </italic>'of Rome'-Old Lithuanian <italic toggle="yes">Rymas</italic>, Mod. Lith. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">Roma </italic>'Rome'. <sentence_start/>Regarding origin, range and use of these plants one misses a clear motivation for this label [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B12" count="1">12</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Generally, <italic toggle="yes">ridikas </italic>refers to any tap-root, <italic toggle="yes">ropė </italic>names turnip, tubers, knobs-roots as well as fruits.

The origin of <italic toggle="yes">D. stramonium </italic>is not clear as mentioned above, but Rome is no serious option. <sentence_start/>For <italic toggle="yes">Scopolia carniolica </italic>the species designation <italic toggle="yes">carniolica </italic>refers to its origin respectively area of first description in Carniola. <sentence_start/>Russian belladonna occurs wild in the Carpathians, Caucasus, Alps [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B11" count="1">11</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Others note its spreading from the Apennine peninsula to East Europe [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B13" count="1">13</citation>] and a cultivation in Lithuania, Latvia and East Prussia and its use as narcotica, aphrodisiaca and for healing nervous fits [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B14" count="1">14</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, <italic toggle="yes">S. carniolica </italic>has not even been mentioned by Dagys [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B6" count="1">6</citation>]. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">Atropa bella-donna </italic>grows wild in most parts of Europe, South East Asia and North Africa [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B13" count="1">13</citation>]. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">Matricaria recutita </italic>is an indigenous plant to Lithuania, now rather rare [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B15" count="1">15</citation>].

The species of the family <italic toggle="yes">Solanaceae </italic>under discussion have in common that they are introduced to Lithuania. <sentence_start/>That would it make possible to receive a geographic attribute as, to give an example, <italic toggle="yes">graikiškas riešutas </italic>'Greek nut' <italic toggle="yes">Juglans regia </italic>L. did. <sentence_start/>The latter agrees with the way the plant was cultivated and spread. <sentence_start/>The Persian Walnut is very often attributed with geographical terms [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B2" count="1">2</citation>]. <sentence_start/>On the contrary, the plants attributed in <italic toggle="yes">Rymo </italic>have no names in neighbouring languages referring to their origin, except Russian belladonna with a different localization, however. <sentence_start/>A recent study has shown that common Lithuanian plant names-not book names-refer very seldom to the geographic origin of the plant [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B16" count="1">16</citation>].

We suggest that <italic toggle="yes">rymo </italic>(genitive of <italic toggle="yes">rymas</italic>) has nothing in common with Rome. <sentence_start/>It is by accident phonetically equal to the Old Lithuanian name of Rome: <italic toggle="yes">Rymas</italic>. <sentence_start/>Therefore the option to reinterpret the meaning of the word-a folk etymology-has been given. <sentence_start/>But what is the origin of <italic toggle="yes">rymo</italic>? <sentence_start/>Have a look on data of Lithuanian lexicology and folklore.

A once popular Lithuanian game is named "<italic toggle="yes">ropę rauti</italic>" 'to root out the turnip' [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B17" count="1">17</citation>]. <sentence_start/>One actor explains that his wife has a violent urge for <italic toggle="yes">Rymo ridikas</italic>, therefore it should be rooted out right now [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B18" count="1">18</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Another version requires <italic toggle="yes">trimo lapo </italic>'stanching leaf', because the actor has been bitten by a dog.

The urge for <italic toggle="yes">Rymo ridikas </italic>appears in phrases such as <italic toggle="yes">Užsigeidė kaip bobutė Rymo ridiko </italic>'She demands rymo turnip like an old woman' [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B17" count="1">17</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Noteworthy, in all versions of the phrases female persons require it. <sentence_start/>This circumstance makes it less convincing to argue with narcotica in this special case. <sentence_start/>The game is typical for wedding ceremonies, the man is looking for medicine for a female person. <sentence_start/>It could be supposed that the game was the modelling of birth and asking for the midwife. <sentence_start/>Therefore-asking the midwife-special phrases have been used, straightforward terms like child giving or birth were to avoided, usual encodings were e.g. <italic toggle="yes">pečius sugriuvo </italic>'the stove tumbles down', <italic toggle="yes">gandras atnešė broliuką </italic>'the stork delivered a brother' [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B19" count="1">19</citation>].

<italic toggle="yes">Scopolia carniolica </italic>and <italic toggle="yes">Hyoscyamus niger </italic>are known for traditional use aborning to soothe the pain in labour [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B9" count="1">9</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B20" count="1">20</citation>]. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">D. stramonium </italic>and <italic toggle="yes">A. bella-donna </italic>are also anodynes. <sentence_start/>Data on real or possible use of the latter both species while child giving we did not observe. <sentence_start/>All plants in <italic toggle="yes">rymo </italic>are officinal ones. <sentence_start/>Lithuanian <italic toggle="yes">raminti </italic>'to calm, quieten; soothe; console; ease pain' is a favourite word to express soothing. <sentence_start/>Related words are e.g. Lithuanian <italic toggle="yes">ryma </italic>'tranquility, calm', <italic toggle="yes">rymoti </italic>'to think, meditate', <italic toggle="yes">ramus </italic>'quiet' [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B8" count="1">8</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B10" count="1">10</citation>]. <sentence_start/>There is no hindrance to integrate <italic toggle="yes">Rymo </italic>and all of the plant names into this word family.

<italic toggle="yes">Rymo ramunė </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">Matricaria recutita</italic>' is said to ease pain in the stomach: <italic toggle="yes">ramuliai vidų ramina </italic>[<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B10" count="1">10</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Therefore, we suppose that not only <italic toggle="yes">rymo </italic>but also <italic toggle="yes">ramunė </italic>belongs to the family of <italic toggle="yes">rimti </italic>'to became quiet, calm' as well. <sentence_start/>Linguists claim that Lithuanian <italic toggle="yes">ramunė </italic>etc. and others like Russian <italic toggle="yes">romaška </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">Matricaria </italic>spp. etc.' goes back to Latin <italic toggle="yes">anthemis romana</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">chamaemelum romanum </italic>[<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B8" count="1">8</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B21" count="1">21</citation>].

However, the origin of this Latin name shows that it has nothing in common with Rome. <sentence_start/>Marzell [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B2" count="1">2</citation>] notes that <italic toggle="yes">romanum </italic>only means 'not native' here; but this is not the point. <sentence_start/>He remarks further that the claim mentioned by Mattioli in 1600 "the species grows around Timur near Rome" triggered off the use of <italic toggle="yes">romanum</italic>. <sentence_start/>In fact, it did not grow there at this time, it was unknown to authors of antiquity [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B2" count="1">2</citation>]. <sentence_start/>So, why did Mattioli claim this? <sentence_start/>The answer lies in this case in common German names, e.g. <italic toggle="yes">Romei, Remey </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">Matricaria </italic>spp., <italic toggle="yes">Chamaemelum </italic>spp.' <sentence_start/>Relating the name which sounds like Rome to Rome is a usual linguistic process named folk etymology, the same as we report for Lithuanian <italic toggle="yes">Rymo</italic>.

The situation with the Russian material is very similar. <sentence_start/>Merkulova [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B21" count="1">21</citation>] notes Russian <italic toggle="yes">cvetu romanova </italic>'Roman flower' and <italic toggle="yes">romanova trava </italic>'Roman herb' found in written sources from 1534. <sentence_start/>She claims that Middle Age Latin called the plants <italic toggle="yes">anthemis romanum, chamaemelum roman</italic>, unfortunately without giving evidence for this claim. <sentence_start/>This would classify the names as pure book names. <sentence_start/>The Russian and Polish spelling of Rome is with <italic toggle="yes">i </italic>or <italic toggle="yes">y</italic>. <sentence_start/>Versions with <italic toggle="yes">o </italic>are quite new-from the 20<sup>th </sup>century. <sentence_start/>So we have the strange situation that Russian <italic toggle="yes">rimskaja romaška </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">Chamaemelum nobile</italic>' would point to Rome in both parts. <sentence_start/>The older one (<italic toggle="yes">romaška</italic>) would show the modern spelling of Rome. <sentence_start/>The new one, which is indeed a translation from a binary (Latin) plant name, shows the traditional spelling.

Therefore we conclude that Russian <italic toggle="yes">romaška </italic>as well as Lithuanian <italic toggle="yes">rymo</italic>, German <italic toggle="yes">Romei </italic>refers to the healing properties of <italic toggle="yes">Matricaria recutita</italic>. <sentence_start/>All these plant names should be cognate to each other. <sentence_start/>Similar plant names in <italic toggle="yes">rymo </italic>for <italic toggle="yes">Atropa bella-donna, Scopolia carniolica </italic>and <italic toggle="yes">Datura stramonium</italic>, on the one hand, and <italic toggle="yes">Matricaria recutita</italic>, on the other hand, result from the use of <italic toggle="yes">rimti </italic>for both, haemostatic effort on wounds (cf. <sentence_start/>German <italic toggle="yes">die Blutung einer Wunde stillen </italic>'to staunch a wound' where <italic toggle="yes">still </italic>means 'calm, quiet') and the effort on the psyche.
Dagys

Lithuanian plant names containing the stem <italic toggle="yes">dag</italic>- or <italic toggle="yes">deg</italic>- may belong to one of three different concepts. <sentence_start/>However, only one of them is taken into consideration usually i.e. the concept of thornes, spines and prickles: Lithuanian <italic toggle="yes">dagys </italic>and <italic toggle="yes">dagilis </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">Carduus </italic>spp., <italic toggle="yes">Cirsium </italic>spp., <italic toggle="yes">Onopordum acanthium </italic>L., <italic toggle="yes">Silybum marianum </italic>Gaerth.', <italic toggle="yes">dagišius </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">Xanthium spinosum </italic>L.', <italic toggle="yes">dyguldagis </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">Datura stramonium </italic>L.' [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B6" count="1">6</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B8" count="1">8</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B10" count="1">10</citation>]. <sentence_start/>One more example, where <italic toggle="yes">dag</italic>- refers to the concept of thorns or the like are <italic toggle="yes">dagutis</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">diegiažolė</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">dygulis </italic>etc. <sentence_start/>'<italic toggle="yes">Geum urbanum </italic>L.'. <sentence_start/>The plant has no thorns but the fruit is prickly like burdock's one. <sentence_start/>Lithuanian <italic toggle="yes">velniadagis </italic>'diablo's prick' names <italic toggle="yes">Arctium </italic>sp.

The second concept refers to Lith. <italic toggle="yes">degti </italic>'to burn' [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B22" count="1">22</citation>]. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">Deguèiukas </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">Lychnis viscaria </italic>(L.) K. Jess' is related as well. <sentence_start/>This name, however, should be seen in relation to the use of stalks made from <italic toggle="yes">Lychnis </italic>spp. for candle wicks [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B2" count="1">2</citation>]. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">Lychnis </italic>had been derived from the Greek name for light as well [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B3" count="1">3</citation>].

A third concept has been introduced recently [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B7" count="1">7</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B23" count="1">23</citation>]. <sentence_start/>It is similar to the preceding one. <sentence_start/>It refers to a use as incense especially in healing.

Additionally, Lithuanian <italic toggle="yes">dagilis </italic>appears in refrains of of Lithuanian folk songs "<italic toggle="yes">Lio lelijėla, lio dagilio; Lelijėla, dagilio</italic>", "<italic toggle="yes">Dobile, dogile, Dobile, totata</italic>" [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B23" count="1">23</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Here, the term is connected with other plant names: <italic toggle="yes">lelija </italic>'lily' and <italic toggle="yes">dobilas </italic>'clover'. <sentence_start/>It is very difficult to find out which species is meant by <italic toggle="yes">dagilis</italic>. <sentence_start/>As we can exclude any reference to thorns, it seems possible to suggest a use as incense, e.g. for healing purposes.

In order to heal the folk illness timorousness (Lithuanian <italic toggle="yes">išgąstis</italic>) the patient is smoked with seeds of <italic toggle="yes">Datura stramonium </italic>L., flowers of <italic toggle="yes">Paeonia </italic>spp. and <italic toggle="yes">dagis </italic>[<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B9" count="1">9</citation>], with dry grinded <italic toggle="yes">dagiliai </italic>[<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B24" count="1">24</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The identity of the latter-<italic toggle="yes">dagis </italic>and <italic toggle="yes">dagiliai</italic>-remains unclear.

Different interpretations seem applicably for <italic toggle="yes">durnadagis, dyguldagis </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">Datura stramonium</italic>'. <sentence_start/>It has been named thorn apple with respect to its thorny fruit. <sentence_start/>The use as incense has been attested: throwing <italic toggle="yes">D. stramonium </italic>on the hot sauna oven has been an erotically charged joke somewhere in rural Lithuania [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B11" count="1">11</citation>,<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B25" count="1">25</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Common German plant names <italic toggle="yes">Rauchöffelkraut, Asthmakraut </italic>'<italic toggle="yes">D. stramonium</italic>' [<citation ref-type="bibr" rid="B2" count="1">2</citation>] refers also to healing properties.

Common names of <italic toggle="yes">Potentilla erecta </italic>(L.) Raeusch. are beyond question. <sentence_start/><italic toggle="yes">Degimai </italic>'burning', <italic toggle="yes">degimo žolė </italic>'burning herb', <italic toggle="yes">degsnys </italic>'burnt place' refer to words for burning; <italic toggle="yes">dagiai </italic>and <italic toggle="yes">dagiukas </italic>are suspected to do so as well. <sentence_start/>The plant was used as incense as can be seen from its name <italic toggle="yes">priemetžolė </italic>'herb for nervous fits'. <sentence_start/>The illness <italic toggle="yes">priemėtis </italic>is widely healed smoking herbs.
Conclusion

Plants may-according to use and habit-belong to different ethnotaxa. <sentence_start/>This has been shown for three Lithuanian categories, each of them containing <italic toggle="yes">Datura stramonium</italic>. <sentence_start/>The affinity of a certain plant to a category is sensitive to the language used in the name-giving process-only a language where one word is appropriate for stanching wounds, easing pain and calming the psyche may group <italic toggle="yes">Atropa bella-donna, Scopolia carniolica, Datura stramonium </italic>and <italic toggle="yes">Matricaria recutita </italic>together.
